questions.stem: Which Part and Articles of the Indian Constitution deal with the Official Language of the Union?

options.option_text: Part XVI, Articles 330–342
Part XVII, Articles 343–351
Part XVIII, Articles 352–360
Part XIV, Articles 308–323

questions.explanation: Part XVII of the Constitution (Articles 343–351) deals with Official Language. Article 343 designates Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union; English was allowed for 15 years after commencement (until 1965) and continues by Parliamentary law.

questions.stem: How many languages are currently listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?

options.option_text: 18 languages
14 languages
22 languages
25 languages

questions.explanation: The Eighth Schedule originally listed 14 languages. Sindhi was added in 1967 (21st Amendment); Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali in 1992 (71st Amendment); and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali in 2004 (92nd Amendment), bringing the total to 22.

questions.stem: Article 351 of the Constitution directs the Union to promote the spread of Hindi. Which two language families should Hindi draw vocabulary from, as specified in this Article?

options.option_text: Urdu (primarily) and Arabic-Persian classical traditions
Tamil and Telugu as the oldest Dravidian language families
English and French as the dominant international languages
Sanskrit (primarily) and other languages of the Eighth Schedule

questions.explanation: Article 351 directs the Union to promote Hindi so it can serve as a medium of expression for India's composite culture, drawing primarily from Sanskrit and secondarily from forms, style, and expressions used in Hindustani and other languages of the Eighth Schedule, without displacing other languages.

questions.stem: The Official Languages Act, 1963 (amended 1967) allows English to continue as an associate official language even after 1965. Which states' opposition primarily prompted the 1967 amendment that made this guarantee permanent?

options.option_text: Tamil Nadu (then Madras State) anti-Hindi agitation
West Bengal protests over Bengali language recognition
Punjab's Punjabi Suba demand for a separate language state
Andhra Pradesh agitation for Telugu official status

questions.explanation: The 1965 anti-Hindi agitation in Madras State (now Tamil Nadu) — in which students and activists protested the planned replacement of English by Hindi — led to significant unrest. The 1967 amendment to the Official Languages Act guaranteed that English would continue as an associate language as long as any non-Hindi state wished, effectively giving non-Hindi states a veto.

questions.stem: Which constitutional provision protects linguistic minorities by requiring states to provide instruction in the mother tongue at the primary education stage?

options.option_text: Article 30 — right of minorities to establish educational institutions
Article 29 — protection of interests of minorities generally
Article 350A — primary education in mother tongue for linguistic minorities
Article 343 — official language of the Union being Hindi (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Article 350A (inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956) requires states and local authorities to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minority groups. Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

questions.stem: The three-language formula recommended for school education in India requires students to learn which combination of languages?

options.option_text: Hindi, Sanskrit, and one classical language from the Eighth Schedule
The regional language, Hindi, and English (in non-Hindi states)
English, one Dravidian language, and one Indo-Aryan language
The state's official language, Urdu, and one North Indian language

questions.explanation: The three-language formula (first recommended by the Official Language Commission 1956, later by National Policy on Education 1968 and 1986) stipulates: In Hindi-speaking states — Hindi, English, and a modern Indian language (preferably southern); In non-Hindi states — the regional language, Hindi, and English. Its implementation has been uneven, as Tamil Nadu officially follows a two-language policy.

questions.stem: Which language was the last to be added to the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, bringing the total to 22?

options.option_text: Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali — added together in 1992
Sindhi — added as the 15th language in 1967 (alternative interpretation)
Sanskrit — added after independence as a classical literary language
Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali — all added simultaneously in 2004

questions.explanation: The 92nd Constitutional Amendment (2004) added four languages simultaneously: Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali — bringing the Eighth Schedule total to 22. Prior to this, the 71st Amendment (1992) had added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali (17→20), and the 21st Amendment (1967) had added Sindhi (15→16).
